rows.what the ink shows: Inside the parentheses is one short upright stroke, slightly inclined, with no upper and lower lobes of a 3. Both enclosing parentheses remain separate.
The isolated glyph after pour has an upright ascender crossed by a short horizontal bar, with a small lower continuation. It is a crossed t, unlike the uncrossed V-shaped nu in the integral below.

After the looped d, the next glyph descends to a pointed low vertex and rises in a slanted right arm ending in a short outward hook. There is no transverse bar or extra stem; the following parenthesis is separate.

The small cancelled subscript lies to the right of the long phi descender. An upper upright and short crossing stroke survive, but several heavy zigzag cancellation strokes cover the body and lower return, so they do not securely distinguish an f.

The word has a low initial series of joined strokes, a pronounced q descender, and a rising terminal ue tail. The pen stops before a clear gap to the following word; no additional ment sequence follows.

The final letter is a small open e form with an acute accent above it. The ink ends immediately after that accented e, with clear paper to its right; no second terminal e is present. The initial d loop and tall t also remain visible.

Despite the horizontal cancellation through its baseline, the initial tall loop, the f ascender, several separate i dots, and the later tall t with the short final ion group remain visible above the stroke.

The cancelled leading letter retains an upper loop, a long descending stem and a short lower turn. To its right is a smaller star made from intersecting short strokes, below the top loop of f; the diagonal deletion strokes pass across both without removing those features.

An initial s-like turn, a low p stroke and a joined rounded group survive on the left. Two long cancelling strokes merge with the rest of the word, leaving isolated ascenders but obscuring the internal letters and final ending needed to establish spectralement.

At the left end of the cancelled line, the first letter has a tall curved upper portion and a lower rightward turn. A separate short i stroke and dot follow it before the next word. The cancelling line crosses their feet but leaves these features visible.

The proposed E occupies the small rounded group after Si. Its upper loop and low rightward continuation survive, but the middle and lower portions coincide with the thick cancellation, preventing a secure three-part E reading or a different segmentation.

In the proposed est un group, a short upper bar, a sloping hooked stroke and a later upright remain above or below the cancelling line. The connections and low letter bodies are merged into the deletion, so neither the s/t division nor both letters of un can be recovered securely.

The right-hand residue is covered by parallel heavy horizontal strokes and a long enclosing return. Only a few upper humps and tiny lower remnants survive; they do not provide a recoverable word sequence.

The upper slant and left vertex of a less-than shape are visible. Its entire lower portion is a dense retraced black block, with no clean white gap to determine whether a separate equality bar lies below the lower arm.

The deleted expression retains a broad phi loop, its long downward stem, and separate parentheses around the crossed t. The paper immediately below and to the right of the phi stem is clear: there is no separate small f stem or crossbar there. The diagonal and horizontal deletion strokes run through the main glyph and argument.

The cancelled text under the inserted right-hand limit has a few visible dots, short ascenders and a terminal rightward fragment. A thick horizontal deletion covers the x-height and connections of the phrase, so the complete word sequence continuité à droite cannot be established from the surviving ink.

The insertion begins with the large initial A-like turn and the compressed dotted ending of Ainsi, then the separated low on group. In identifie the d loop, crossed t, tall f stroke and following i dot stand above the low connected letters; the final e tail is distinct from the curved insertion underline.
